chapter: Dance tastes, big bands and the boat
title: Pit work, Club Forest, the Edgewater and convention jobs in the early 1940s
summary: Asked about changing public taste, DeDroit describes his years as stock-company leader and theater second trumpet, then Suburban Gardens, Club Forest and the Edgewater in Biloxi.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: Okay. How would you contrast the public taste in music, especially in New Orleans, as it changed during the years from the first that you remember to about 1930? What kind of music did people seem to want in those years, at various times?

Well, for a little while I was not a leader. I had been leading the orchestra for St. Charles. It was a dramatic stock company. Two matinees a week. Oh, it was a darling job. And I decided I would take a rest to get my lip a rest. So the only time I'd know what was going on was when I'd go out and they were all playing the same, playing the same music. It's just different tunes. They all play with a beat. And all of them did free radio programs for publicity, including yours truly. And well, it's just hard for me to tell you, but I know that when I went, I was playing at the St. Charles and it was so warm and they had a typhoon fan or something, there'd be more noise than the people on the stage. They closed. But I had them hooked for a two year contract. So they asked me if I would go into the signing I was putting on the public shows, and they gave me more money. They raised my pay. And I was the feature trumpet player and assistant band leader. If the band leader, if the master of ceremonies got sick, I'd take over the show, you know, which I did, direct the show. So it's just like being locked up. You only play their music, you see? And I wouldn't take anything. I was trying to stay in the business. I didn't want to play too much. So I took the job as second trumpet, and featured man on the stage. But in the pit, when we played, Mr. Capira played the first trumpet, an excellent trumpet player, so I had no responsibility except to memorize the show. And so I couldn't tell you what was going on all the while I played at the Sanger. But when I came out of there, I went out to Suburban Guns with the big band. I went back in the show business. And at that time the Club Forest was bringing named bands, all the big bands, and they had the gambling, and all we had was slot machines. We had big stars but we didn't do the business. So they had to get a cheaper band. So then I decided to do strictly commercial, you know, spot jobs we used to call them spot jobs. Here there are conventions and all like that. And subsequently I built it up fine. I was a house band at the Edgewater in Biloxi. I got every convention they ever had over there. And the convention manager at the Roosevelt gave me everything. He could recommend it because I knew how to play. When I played for people who were past 40, I played two beat music.
What years were that, that you're talking about?
Well I guess that was in the early 40s.
